channel.title: Keith Dunstan
channel.description: The collected literary works of Keith Dunstan OAM

item.title: Sandy Stone
item.description: Introduces Sandy Stone, Humphries's second great character, the gentle and profoundly boring ghost of suburban Glen Iris, and traces his origins to a chance encounter on Bondi Beach before examining the creation of Sir Les Patterson, the slobbering cultural attaché.

item.title: The spawning of a rebel
item.description: Traces Barry Humphries's upbringing in Camberwell, his art education under George Bell, his loathing of sport at Melbourne Grammar, his brief university career, and the Dada provocations and nostalgia-soaked Melbourne campaigns of his early years.

item.title: Broadway
item.description: Follows Dame Edna's decades-long conquest of international audiences, from her disastrous New York debut in 1977 to her Tony Award-winning triumph in 2000, and surveys Humphries's private life, his family, his three houses, and his plans for the future.

item.title: More please
item.description: Recounts the decade-long drinking crisis that threatened to end Humphries's career in the 1960s, including his arrest on Burke Road and a savage mugging outside a Richmond factory, before tracing his recovery and his creation of the Barry McKenzie comic strip for Private Eye.

item.title: Edna at fifty
item.description: Charts the creation and evolution of Dame Edna Everage, from her debut at a 1955 Melbourne revue through her transformation into an international megastar, tracing the gladdie song, the sequined gowns, and her conquest of the Apollo Theatre and the world.

item.title: The most important entertainer
item.description: Introduces Barry Humphries as Australia's greatest all-round entertainer, setting out the range of his talent, his uncanny memory, and the ferocious mockery he faced at home before the rest of the world acknowledged his genius.

item.title: Turn That Old Pianola
item.description: An interview with Jack O'Hagan at his Elwood home on the fiftieth anniversary of 'Along the Road to Gundagai', in which he reveals he picked the town's name off a map without ever having visited the place.

item.title: Bazza Arrives on the Silver Screen
item.description: A preview of the forthcoming film "The Adventures of Barry McKenzie" at Sydney University finds Barry Crocker as a lovable ocker innocent amid rapacious Poms, complete with a chunder song, a colour chunder scene, and a supporting cast including Spike Milligan, Peter Cook and Dennis Price.

item.title: It's Been a Very Hard Month
item.description: A report on the five major banquets and three club dinners marking Henry Bolte's retirement, culminating in the 1,200-person Liberal Party dinner at the Royal Ballroom, with a selection of the premier's most quotable farewell remarks.

item.title: Outracing the Race of the Year
item.description: A report on the Ocean Racing Club of Victoria's new Melbourne-to-Hobart yacht race, launching on Boxing Day in direct competition with the Sydney-Hobart, with a defence of Victoria's deeper ocean racing tradition.

item.title: Home Brewers Take the Field
item.description: The home brewing boom that swept Melbourne following Carlton brewery's public objections to amateur beer-making in 1971, with fermenters filling refrigerators and the Olinda kit-maker reporting growth of several hundred percent.

item.title: The Jeanagers
item.description: A visit to Jean City, the new jeans shop in Swanston Street, Melbourne, where Carlton brewery beer-label T-shirts sit alongside Wrangler and Levis, and proprietor David Anderson's philosophy is that anything too fancy would drive customers straight back to Myers.

item.title: Pioneering at $50 a Day
item.description: A visit to Naringal, a stately homestead near Ballarat run by the Rowe family for American tourists, offering colonial pastoral life complete with silver candelabra, kangaroo-spotting, and a tour of the family cemetery.

item.title: Regressors, It's Time to March
item.description: The closure of the Federal Hotel in Collins Street, Melbourne, an 1888 Coffee Palace of sculptured Victorian excess, prompts a call for a Society Against Progress to resist the city's unstoppable appetite for demolition.

item.title: A Grand Vision for Melbourne
item.description: The launch of the Flinders Gate project, a plan to redevelop Melbourne's Flinders Street railway yards into hotels, cinemas and a new station, with the name 'Flinders Gate' winning a public competition after readers submitted suggestions ranging from Ned's Nook to Squizzy's Place.

item.title: Random Notes of a Citizen in Gloom
item.description: Melbourne's SEC power strike of February 1972, observed from the premiere of a new Australian play in darkness to Sir Henry Bolte backing winners at the Pakenham Races while the city's air conditioners and swimming pools sat idle.

item.title: Feed Me Only Rhubarb Jelly
item.description: The Weight Watchers International Christmas party at the Mayfair reception house in Elwood, where 280 members ate strictly 'legal' food, weighed to the ounce, with rhubarb jelly standing in for Christmas pudding.

item.title: Whatever Happened to the Old Cricket Fury?
item.description: A historical survey of passionate cricket fan protests over selection decisions, arguing that the fury sparked by Bill Lawry's axing from the Australian touring team in 1972 is mild compared with the monster indignation meetings, brawling selectors, and prisoner protests of earlier eras.

item.title: Take Me to Your Folk Museum!
item.description: The heritage tourism boom sweeping Victoria's country towns, from Echuca's paddlesteamer wharf to Ballarat's Sovereign Hill, as local councils discover that history and nostalgia make marvellous motel-fillers.

item.title: A New Religion for Winter
item.description: Melbourne's devotion to Australian Rules football described as a full-blown religion, from a widow's request to inter her husband's ashes in Richmond's goal square to the Victorian government's approval of VFL Football Pools and the imminent launch of Tattslotto.

item.title: How Groceries Went Foreign
item.description: Jim Cairns' warning that foreign interests would control half of Australian manufacturing within a decade, illustrated by a walk around a local supermarket where almost nothing from cornflakes to pet food is still Australian-owned.

item.title: Graduates of the Money Game
item.description: A chemistry graduate turned cab driver — one of 14 unemployed out of 18 in his cohort — prompts a proposal for a 'Bachelor of Materialism' degree, with George Frew, Bruce Small, David Wynn and Norman Shierlaw as lecturers, Sir Reginald Ansett as dean, and Sir Henry Bolte conferring degrees.

item.title: Barking About a Bite
item.description: Uncle Ben's launches its new Pal Meaty Bites dog food at the Old Melbourne Motor Inn with a fashion parade inside a giant inflatable dog, a Cinemascope interview, and a banquet for 80 grocery executives and their wives flown in from around Australia.

item.title: Feathering the Top Eagle's Pad
item.description: Melbourne's new wave of luxury city apartment towers, from Michael Edgley's penthouse at Park Towers in Spring Street to the $250,000 24th-floor suite at 99 Spring Street with marble from Greece and tiles from Italy, and the more modest 135-flat Lonsdale Heights for those who prefer their galvanised iron roof-top views.

item.title: A Lovely War at the Werribee Gorge
item.description: Australian units of American Civil War re-enactors camp for four days at the Werribee Gorge near Bacchus Marsh, with muzzle loaders, Confederate uniforms, a Union loyalist doomed to die at every outing, and evidence of Foster's Lager burned black in the campfire.

item.title: Bolte — The last of the Victorians
item.description: A profile of Henry Bolte on his retirement after 17 years as Victorian premier, arguing through assessments from Clyde Holding and Jim McDonald that Bolte's rough, anti-intellectual self-certainty was both his greatest political skill and a perfect mirror for the city he ruled.

item.title: The Siege of Rutherglen
item.description: The Labor Day weekend Rutherglen Wine Festival, when between 15,000 and 20,000 young people descended on the small Victorian wine town of 1200 residents for three days of mass public drinking and police with paddy wagons.

item.title: Evolving the Mayoral Egg
item.description: An examination of Melbourne's arcane system for electing its lord mayor through the Civic Group's private Sunday-night caucus, prompted by the first-ever dropping of an incumbent after one term and the quiet elevation of a former RAAF fighter pilot in his place.

item.title: The Winter of Their Discontent
item.description: Melbourne's warm and snowless June of 1972 leaves ski-resort operators nursing heavy losses, while Keith Dunstan reports from Falls Creek on the fashion designer lodges, ski-gear merchants and the Thai-roofed retreat of the city's 'Duckfeather king.'

item.title: Taking the Bite out of Shark
item.description: Victoria's ban on school shark over 28 inches for food, prompted by mercury contamination, threatens to devastate the fish and chip industry whose 24 million pieces of "flake" a year represent 70 per cent of Victorian fish consumption, and prompts speculation about what to call the shark should it need a new name.
